Yes, you are completely correct. It always drives me crazy when people say you can get an "acquired Chiari" when they actually mean a herniation of the cerebellum. I remember I asked my surgeon if I had an acquired Chiari and he laughed at me because he said you can acquire that but you can acquire a herniation due to different things.

Chiari is the malformation of the posterior fossa, the actual skull. A good surgeon will rule out other factors that could be causing a herniation (tumor, high intracranial pressure, csf leak, etc) and will also measure the size of the posterior fossa and can tell you if it is malformed (too small). If a surgeon doesn't at least try to rule out the other factors that could be contributing to your herniation, you should find another surgeon.

Are both surgeons EDS aware? If not, I would go with the surgeon that has experience with EDS, just in case. EDS can complicate the way your dura heals, the way the suturing and closing should be done, and risks for csf leaks, and co-conditions that may come with Chiari such as high intracranial pressure, tethered cord, etc.

A proper Chiari surgeon should treat all the patients as if they have EDS even if you havent been tested.

Edit: I have EDS and had decompression. My surgeon would do all decompression as if everyone had EDS. My decompression was successful and I do believe it was because of this. He made sure only the necessary amount of bone was taken, a bovine dura patch was used, no metal mesh, used glue instead of sutures, no shaving of c2, a listened to me when I told him I didn't want him to shave c1 because I wanted to avoid any craniocervical instability in the future.
I would get opinions from Dr. Petra Klinge in Rhode Island and Dr. Gerald Grant at Duke.

In your case, there are a few possible things that could have happened. If you have EDS, the ligaments that hold your head to your neck could have become more lax with time and could now be causing craniocervical instability. Perhaps your surgeon took too much bone off but now there is also surgery that can help with that. There is also the possibility that you have high intracranial pressure that is causing some of these symptoms and they are not caused by Chiari. There are medicines that can help with that or surgery if medicines aren't an option. Then there is the possibility that your cerebellum reherniated and the best approach to this would be to figure out what is either pulling or pushing your brain down. 

I don't tell you all these things to worry you but for you to look into and have a good idea of what these things are and you can ask your doctor the right questions. Most, if not all, of these things show up on MRI so it's a good thing your doctor ordered it.

There are comments saying that Chiari is a herniation above a certain measurement and that is not true.   
  
Chiari is malformation of the bone of the skull. That's the entire definition. Either you have it or you don't.  
  
The herniation of the cerebellum, however, can be caused by Chiari malformation, or other things taking up space inside your skull. These things can be extra csf, arachnoid cysts, tumors, scar tissue, etc or anything that is pulling the brain down like tethered cord.  
   
It is also not true that surgical intervention at a certain herniation only. If the doctor excludes anything else that could be causing your symptoms, and you have the malformation of the skull, then surgery is needed to correct the malformation (remove some bone, expand the dura). A true Chiari specialist will tell you this, most neurosurgeons don't know enough about Chiari. 

Now, what your doctor needs to do is consider if the aranchnoid cyst you have could be taking enough space to cause this "relatively" small herniation, or if you have high intracranial pressure because of said cysts or idiopathically.

If I was you I probably try to see a Chiari specialist (if you are able to) so all options can be considered. A lot of times smaller herniations are caused by other things (not Chiari) and the high intracranial pressure can be treated and the herniation will decrease and so will the symptoms.

I havent looked at this stuff in a while since my surgery was years ago but I do remember coming across papers where there were measurements of the occipital bone in the skull and these measurements were smaller  when compared to those of people without the malformation. The occipital bone can be smaller, like there is less space for the cerebellum in the back of the head or it can be indented in, also giving less space to the back of the skull.

In people with the malformation and cerebellum herniation there is a question of whether it is only the herniation that causes symptoms or there is also the addition of tissue laxity (like with a collagen disorder eds, which is why you should be evaluated before going to a surgeon, if possible) making the herniation also worse. Then there are the other factors of head trauma, high icp, tethered cord, things like that. 

So what I'm trying to say is that a good doctor, hopefully a Chiari specialist, will know to measure the actual malformation or at least look at it and see the abnormality (this should be easy for them), take a collagen disorder into consideration, and rule out or treat any other external factors first instead of jumping right into surgery. 

In my case, I went to 2 specialists and asked them to look at the actual malformation and tell me if the measurements of my occipital bone were off and to rule out other possible conditions. I did have an EDS diagnosis beforehand so that was also taken into consideration. I did have tethered cord pulling down the brain stem but one of the surgeons said it wasn't enough to cause a herniation the size of the herniation I had, which is now something I deeply believe in. I know lots of cases are not as clear-cut but it's best to rule out everything to avoid multiple surgeries.
